name: Media
blurb: Generation tools transformed production while training-data litigation transformed the business relationship with AI; cross-linked to the lawsuit tracker.

points.desc: The US Copyright Office AI policy programme, covering registrability of AI-assisted works, training on copyrighted material, and digital replicas, is the primary legal reference for anyone publishing AI-assisted media in the United States.
points.name: The Copyright Office is writing the rules

points.desc: Article 50 of the EU AI Act sets transparency obligations for AI-generated and manipulated content, including deepfakes. It applies to publishers distributing into the EU regardless of where the content was made.
points.name: Synthetic media carries a disclosure duty in the EU

points.desc: C2PA publishes the open technical specification for content credentials: cryptographically signed provenance that travels with an image, video, or audio file. It is the standards-body answer to the question of what a newsroom attaches to a synthetic asset.
points.name: Provenance is being standardised, not invented per outlet

points.desc: The Associated Press documents its own AI use in production, including transcription, shotlisting, and metadata. It is an operating newsroom describing deployed systems rather than a vendor describing a roadmap.
points.name: A wire service publishing what it actually does

points.desc: AP publishes its standards for generative AI in journalism, covering what may be produced with it, what must be verified, and what may not be published. One of the few newsroom policies available to read in full rather than summarised.
points.name: Newsroom rules written down and published

points.desc: The Reuters Institute Digital News Report at Oxford surveys news consumption across dozens of markets, including audience trust in AI-assisted journalism and newsroom adoption. Survey-based and published in full.
points.name: Audience data on AI in news, measured annually

points.desc: The Tow Center for Digital Journalism at Columbia publishes research on algorithmic distribution, newsroom tools, and the business ethics of AI in media, independent of the vendors selling the tools.
points.name: Independent research on newsroom AI tooling

points.desc: The Stanford HAI AI Index tracks technical progress, investment, and adoption annually, with data points covering creative media and journalism. Useful for placing a media-specific claim against the wider trend.
points.name: The field-wide numbers, including creative work

summary: Generation tools transformed production while training-data litigation transformed the business relationship with AI.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey recorded 45.0% of firms in the Information sector reporting AI use in the most recent period, up from 41.9% in the prior period, making it one of the higher-adoption sectors the survey tracks. That figure covers the broad NAICS 51 grouping, which includes broadcasting and publishing alongside software and data services, so the number reflects a range of deployment depths rather than a uniform level of sophistication across every outlet.

Within news production specifically, the Associated Press documents some of the clearest public evidence of what deployed systems actually do. AP uses AI-driven tools to analyze video content and generate shotlists for customers, runs Merlin, an AI-powered search that recognizes elements within photos and videos without relying on descriptions or metadata, and collaborates with AppliedXL to analyze federal registry data and surface actionable news tips to local newsrooms. AP also worked with ShortTok to integrate AI-powered content discovery and video curation into its production workflow. These are described by AP as efficiency and distribution tools rather than replacements for editorial judgment, and the organization states explicitly that it does not see AI as a replacement of journalists in any way.

AP's published standards for generative AI illustrate the governance layer that serious newsrooms are building alongside the tools. Any output from a generative AI tool must be treated as unvetted source material, subject to the same editorial judgment and sourcing standards as any other input. The organization prohibits using generative AI to add or subtract any elements from photos, video, or audio, and will not transmit AI-generated images that are suspected or proven to be false depictions of reality. AP also flags the disinformation risk directly, noting that generative AI makes it easier to spread mis- and disinformation through altered content that may appear entirely realistic, and instructs journalists to apply reverse image search and source verification even to incoming material.

The regulatory environment is taking shape on both sides of the Atlantic, and the obligations are real rather than aspirational. The U.S. Copyright Office has been working through a multi-part AI report since 2023, covering digital replicas in Part 1 published July 31, 2024, the copyrightability of AI-generated outputs in Part 2 published January 29, 2025, and a pre-publication version of Part 3 released May 9, 2025, with no substantive changes expected in its final analysis. The Office received over 10,000 public comments on its notice of inquiry, reflecting the breadth of industry concern about training data and ownership. In the EU, Article 50 of the AI Act requires that synthetic audio, image, video, and text outputs be marked in a machine-readable format detectable as artificially generated, and deployers of deepfake content must disclose that it has been artificially created or manipulated, with limited exceptions for evidently artistic or satirical works. These obligations apply to publishers distributing into the EU regardless of where the content was made.

The technical response to provenance questions is being coordinated at the standards level rather than solved outlet by outlet. The Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity, known as C2PA, publishes an open specification called Content Credentials, described by the organization as functioning like a nutrition label for digital content, providing cryptographically signed provenance information that travels with an image, video, or audio file. The Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism at Oxford surveys audience attitudes toward AI-assisted journalism annually through its Digital News Report, providing a recurring measure of how trust and consumption patterns respond to these changes, and the Tow Center for Digital Journalism at Columbia publishes independent research on newsroom tools and the business ethics of AI in media separate from vendor claims. Active litigation involving AI companies including Perplexity AI, Runway AI, Stability AI, and X.AI is being tracked across more than 100 cases, with copyright and training-data claims most directly relevant to media organizations deciding how to source and license content for AI workflows.
